name: Lena Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We farm three hundred hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape as tenants of the Thornbury estate, and we've held the tenancy for twenty-six years. In November it's the last of the drilling, checking the young crops for slugs, and selling the grain we've got in the store a lorry at a time. My husband Per has a bad back these days, so I do most of the tractor work and he does the books and the selling.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like harvest, the long evenings in the combine when the light goes gold and the whole family's out with trailers. What wears me out is the selling. Per watches the grain price on his phone like it's the football, and if we sell a week too early or too late, that's the profit gone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tractor steers itself on GPS, which I fought against and now wouldn't be without. And now and then I'll ask one of those AI assistants something, like what the weather's doing for spraying or what a new rule means. Per uses it more than me, mostly to argue with it about grain prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the next five years, one at a time. Here's the first. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy and leave it there. I'd tell the women at church it's good for looking up recipes and checking the weather, which is mostly what I use it for. I wouldn't go on about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much. The grain price is set by the world market, the weather does what it likes, and the rent goes up every three years. A clever search engine won't help with any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. I might use the assistant a bit more to help Per with the selling, checking prices and what the big buyers are saying. We'd keep what little we have in the bank, about three weeks of costs, for a bad harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same worries as ever, the weather and the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the rent going up every three years.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate's land agent comes round with his folder and his nice car and tells us what similar farms are paying. It's always more. Last time it went up eight percent, and the wheat price had gone down that year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bad harvest look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twenty twenty-four, it rained through August and we lost a third of the wheat to sprouting in the ear. We sold the old combine and hired a contractor for the next year. We're still paying for that year, really.

S0.say: I'd say it's handy and leave it there. I'd tell the women at church it's good for recipes and checking the weather.
S0.think: I really think it doesn't change much. The world market sets the grain price, the weather does what it likes, and the rent rises every three years.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and uses the AI assistant a bit more to help Per check grain prices and buyers. Keeps the small reserve of about three weeks of costs for a bad harvest.
S0.feel: Calm, with the same worries as ever about weather and rent.
S0.quote: The estate's land agent comes round with his folder and his nice car and tells us what similar farms are paying. It's always more.
S0.fieldNote: She uses AI lightly and matter-of-factly, mostly for weather and recipes. Her real pressures are the three-yearly rent review and a bad harvest they're still paying for. Per's back problem means she does the heavy work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how it should be, slow and careful, so we can see what works before we put money in. I'd say farming has always been about patience. And I'd say young people should still learn the land properly, from family, before any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's fine for us, we'll be handing over before it matters much. But fewer beginners worries me, because our grandson Erik wants to farm, and if the farms round here take fewer young people, he'll only have us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take Erik on properly, as a sort of apprentice, maybe from the next harvest. I'd watch what the big farm next door does with any new tools and try them a year later if they worked. I'd ask the estate whether Erik could be added to the tenancy, which would take some persuading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. It's slow enough to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Erik.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's nineteen and he's been on the farm every summer since he was small. He drove a tractor at twelve, carefully, with Per in the cab. He says he wants to farm, and he means it, he's the one who asks about soil when everyone else is on their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the estate feel about adding Erik?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agent will say they're reviewing all tenancies, they always say that. But the old Lord Thornbury liked families staying on. His son's more of a businessman, so I'd have to show Erik's serious, with a plan on paper.

S1.say: I'd say slow and careful is right, so we can see what works before spending. Young people should still learn the land from family before any machine.
S1.think: I really think we'll hand over before it matters, but fewer beginners worries me. Our grandson Erik wants to farm, and fewer local farm jobs would leave him only us.
S1.do: Takes Erik on as a kind of apprentice from the next harvest. Watches the big farm next door try new tools and follows a year later, and asks the estate to add Erik to the tenancy with a written plan.
S1.feel: Mostly hopeful, because it's slow enough to plan for.
S1.quote: He says he wants to farm, and he means it, he's the one who asks about soil when everyone else is on their phones.
S1.fieldNote: Her steady nature shows in waiting a year behind the neighbour. Everything is about passing the farm to her grandson Erik. Family succession is at the heart of her traditional values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for people in offices, but they'll need to work hard and find new jobs, like people always have. I'd say politicians arguing gets nobody anywhere. I'd say families and churches should look after their own first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the estate office is where it'd hit us. The land agent's job could be done by a machine, and a machine would put the rent up without even coming to look at the farm. And Per's sister does accounts for a builder, and she'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure Erik's tenancy plan was on paper and in front of the estate before anything changed there, maybe in the first six months. I'd use the assistant a bit more myself, to check what the estate's numbers say, so I'm not outdone. And I'd tell Per's sister she's welcome to come and do our books if she needs work, we'd pay her what we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like the idea of a machine deciding our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a machine would put the rent up without coming to look. What would it miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd miss that the field by the river floods every winter and grows nothing in a wet year. The agent knows that, because I've walked him through it in wellies. A machine just sees hectares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay Per's sister what you could. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly, maybe a day a week. But Per's back is getting worse and the books take him longer, so it'd help us too. Family should help family, and it goes both ways.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shame for office people, but they'll need to work hard and find new jobs as people always have. Arguing politicians get nowhere, and families and churches should look after their own first.
S2.think: I really think it would hit us through the estate office, where a machine could raise the rent without seeing the farm. Per's sister, who does accounts for a builder, would be worried too.
S2.do: Puts Erik's tenancy plan in front of the estate within six months. Uses the AI assistant more to check the estate's numbers and offers Per's sister a paid day a week on the farm books.
S2.feel: Uneasy at the idea of a machine deciding their rent.
S2.quote: It'd miss that the field by the river floods every winter and grows nothing in a wet year.
S2.fieldNote: She worries about an AI estate office setting rent with no local knowledge, like the flooding field. Her response is self-help and family, true to her traditional views. She'd use AI defensively, steady rather than eager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say all this talk about who gets the gains is a distraction, people need to get back to work and look after each other. I'd say the land and food matter more than ever when everything else is up in the air. I'd say that at church and at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the rent review that frightens me. When the shares and houses boom, it's not me that gets rich. It's the landlord, and he'll want it back at the rent review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the estate early, well before the next review, with Erik's plan and our records, to show we're good tenants worth keeping. I'd cut back hard, no new machinery, maybe sell the spare trailer. And I'd ask the women at church whether anyone's family needed help, because there'll be a lot of hurting people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the first time the tenancy feels shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the estate in that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've farmed this land well for twenty-six years, never missed a rent day, and our grandson wants to carry it on. I'd say a family on the land is worth more than a few extra pounds a hectare. Whether the young Lord listens is another matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said who gets the gains is a distraction. But the gains going to the landlord is exactly your worry. Isn't that the same thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. Maybe it is. I suppose I don't like the shouting, but I do care who ends up with the land. Put it that way, then.

S3.say: I'd say arguing over the gains is a distraction and people should get back to work and look after each other. Land and food matter more than ever when everything's uncertain.
S3.think: I'm privately frightened of the rent review. When shares and houses boom, the landlord gets rich, not us, and he'll want it back in rent.
S3.do: Goes to the estate early with Erik's plan and their records to show they're good tenants. Cuts back hard, buys no new machinery, may sell the spare trailer, and asks at church who needs help.
S3.feel: Anxious, with the tenancy feeling shaky for the first time.
S3.quote: When the shares and houses boom, it's not me that gets rich. It's the landlord, and he'll want it back at the rent review.
S3.fieldNote: When I gently pointed out the contradiction, she accepted it: she dislikes the shouting but cares who owns the land. The rent review is her real threat in this picture. She'd show up early, records in hand, to make the case for family tenants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming has always changed and good farmers change with it, carefully. I'd say robots should help families stay on the land, not push them off. And I'd say the estate should give tenants who invest a longer lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think self-driving tractors and robots would be all over the big grain farms within a couple of years. The estate might decide one big robot farm pays more rent than three families. That's the thing that'd keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the robots on the big farm next door for a season, then look at hiring a contractor who uses them rather than buying my own. I'd get Erik trained on them, maybe a course at the college, so he's the one who knows how they work. And I'd push the estate hard for a longer lease, in return for us investing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but not beaten. We've seen off bad years before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a contractor rather than buying your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a robot tractor would cost more than we make in five years, and we'd never pay it off before I retire. A contractor carries the risk. Let him worry about it breaking down in the middle of drilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Erik, if the estate chose a robot farm instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm sorry and that it's not his fault. Then I'd tell him to go and work for whoever runs the robots and learn every bit of it, because one day someone will need a farmer who knows both. I'd mean it, though it'd break my heart.

S4.say: I'd say good farmers change carefully, and robots should help families stay on the land, not push them off. The estate should give tenants who invest a longer lease.
S4.think: I really think robot tractors would spread across big grain farms within a couple of years. The estate might decide one robot farm pays more rent than three families.
S4.do: Watches the robots on the farm next door for a season, then hires a contractor who uses them instead of buying one. Gets Erik trained on robots at the college and presses the estate for a longer lease in return for investing.
S4.feel: Alarmed but not beaten, because they've seen off bad years before.
S4.quote: The estate might decide one big robot farm pays more rent than three families.
S4.fieldNote: Her steady approach shows in hiring a robot contractor rather than buying. Her biggest fear is the estate choosing one robot farm over families. Her advice to Erik shows a practical, loving realism.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because that's when the estate could decide it doesn't need families at all. What would help is tenancy law that gives families like ours longer leases and first refusal. And proper apprenticeships, so lads like Erik can learn both the land and the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the church, and the village. If the families go off the land, the church empties and the school shuts. Farming's not just a job here, it's what holds the place together.

headlineQuote: When the shares and houses boom, it's not me that gets rich. It's the landlord, and he'll want it back at the rent review.
portrait: Lena is 58 and farms three hundred hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape as a tenant of the Thornbury estate, doing most of the tractor work because her husband Per has a bad back. She uses AI now and then for the weather and the selling, and believes in hard work, family and church. Every picture comes back to the tenancy and her grandson Erik, who wants to farm. In the fast picture she fears the landlord will take the boom out of her rent, and in the robot picture she fears the estate choosing one robot farm over three families. She'd answer carefully, with a contractor and a longer lease, not a loan.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because the estate might decide it doesn't need tenant families at all.
whatWouldHelp: Tenancy law giving families longer leases and first refusal, and apprenticeships so young people like Erik can learn the land and the machines.
